title: INFWAD – HTML, CSS & JavaScript
description: Theorievragen in de stijl van de sample exam over de lesstof Fundamentals 1 t/m 4: HTML en de DOM, CSS, layout en JavaScript. Vragen, antwoorden en uitleg zijn in het Engels.

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text: What is the primary function of HTML?
questions.explanation: HTML structures content (headings, paragraphs, links, forms). CSS handles style and layout, JavaScript handles interactivity.

options.text: To structure content on a web page
To determine the visual style and layout of a page
To add interactivity to a web page
To manage the database of a website

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text: Which statement about HTML is correct?
questions.explanation: HTML is not a programming language. It uses elements to tell the browser what the content is: text, images, links, inputs, and so on.

options.text: HTML is a programming language that the browser compiles before showing the page
HTML is a styling language that decides colours, fonts and spacing
HTML is a markup language that uses elements (tags) to describe the structure of content
HTML is a scripting language that runs on the server before the page is sent

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text: Which markup is the most semantic way to build the main navigation of a site?
questions.explanation: `<header>` and `<nav>` describe what the block is, the list groups related links, and `<a>` is the element for navigation.

options.text:
`
  • Home
`

`
Home
`

Home

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text: Which of the following is **not** a benefit of using semantic HTML elements like `<nav>`, `<main>` and `<footer>`?
questions.explanation: Semantic elements help accessibility, search engines and maintainability. They do not change how fast CSS is parsed.

options.text: Screen readers can announce the structure of the page to the user
The page renders faster because the browser can skip parsing the CSS
Search engines can better understand what is important on the page
Other developers can understand the structure of the code at a glance

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text:
```html
Save
``` What is the main problem with this element?
questions.explanation: For something interactive you should use `<button>`. A clickable `<div>` works with a mouse, but keyboard users and screen readers lose out.

options.text: A `<div>` cannot have a click handler, so `save()` never runs
The class name `btn` is reserved by the browser for native buttons
Text inside a `<div>` cannot be styled, so the button will be invisible
It is not a real button, so it is not reachable with the keyboard and screen readers don't announce it as a button

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text: When should you use an `<a>` element instead of a `<button>`?
questions.explanation: Use `<a>` for navigation and `<button>` for actions (save, delete, open a menu).

options.text: When the element has to look like a link instead of a button
When the action should work without JavaScript
When the element contains an icon instead of text
When clicking it navigates to another page or location

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text:
```html
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com">
```
What does connecting the label to the input (`for` + `id`) do?
questions.explanation: A connected label makes the input easier to use and accessible. A placeholder does neither of these things.

options.text: It validates that the user typed a valid email address
It hides the placeholder as soon as the label is visible
It sends the label text along with the form data to the server
Clicking the label focuses the input, and screen readers read the label when the input gets focus

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text: Why is it a good idea to place the links of a navigation menu inside a `<ul>` with `<li>` items?
questions.explanation: Grouping related items in a list gives them meaning: a screen reader says e.g. "list, 3 items".

options.text: Because links outside a list are not clickable in some browsers
Because a screen reader announces it as a list with a number of items, so the user knows how many links there are
Because `<ul>` automatically places the links horizontally next to each other
Because search engines ignore links that are not inside a list

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text: What is the DOM?
questions.explanation: The browser parses the HTML into a tree of nodes: the Document Object Model. It lives in memory and is how JavaScript talks to the page.

options.text: A tree of objects in memory that the browser builds from the HTML, which JavaScript can read and change
The HTML file as it is stored on the server
A copy of the CSS that the browser uses to calculate the layout
A browser cache that stores pages so they load faster next time

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text: You run `document.querySelector('h1').textContent = 'Changed!'` in the console. The page updates. Then you open *View page source*. What do you see in the `<h1>`?
questions.explanation: View page source shows the file from the server. The Elements tab shows the live DOM. JavaScript never changes the file on the server.

options.text: The original text, because JavaScript changes the DOM in memory, not the HTML file
`Changed!`, because the DOM and the source are the same thing
Nothing, because the `<h1>` was removed and replaced by a new element
An error, because the source can't be shown after the DOM has been changed

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text: In which order does the browser roughly turn an HTML response into something you can see?
questions.explanation: Parse, style, layout, paint.

options.text: Parse HTML into the DOM → apply CSS → calculate where every box goes → paint pixels
Paint pixels → apply CSS → parse HTML → calculate layout
Apply CSS → parse HTML → paint pixels → calculate layout
Calculate layout → parse HTML → paint pixels → apply CSS

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text: According to the lessons, what is the basic shape of every interactive web page?
questions.explanation: Find a node (`querySelector`), listen for an event (`addEventListener`), change a node (`textContent`, `classList`, ...). Frameworks build on top of this loop.

options.text: Load the data, compile the page, send it to the server
Create a component, mount it, unmount it
Find a node, listen for an event, change a node
Request a page, reload the page, cache the page

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text: What is the difference between `document.querySelector('.item')` and `document.querySelectorAll('.item')`?
questions.explanation: Both use CSS selector syntax. `querySelector` gives the first match (or `null`), `querySelectorAll` gives a list of all matches.

options.text: `querySelector` returns the first matching element, `querySelectorAll` returns all matching elements
`querySelector` searches by class, `querySelectorAll` searches by id
`querySelector` returns a copy of the element, `querySelectorAll` returns the real elements
There is no difference, `querySelectorAll` is the older name

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text:
```html
<button id="calculate">Calculate</button>
<script>
  const button = document.querySelector('#calc');
  button.addEventListener('click', calculate);
</script>
```
What happens?
questions.explanation: There is no element with id `calc`, so `button` is `null`, and `null.addEventListener(...)` throws a TypeError in the console.

options.text: The button works, because `#calc` is a partial match of `calculate`
The click handler is added to the whole document instead
Nothing, the browser silently ignores selectors that don't match
`querySelector` returns `null`, so calling `addEventListener` throws an error

questions.title: Fundamentals 1 – HTML & DOM
questions.text: Why is `element.addEventListener('click', handler)` preferred over `<button onclick="handler()">`?
questions.explanation: `onclick` still works, but keeping behaviour out of the HTML is the modern, more maintainable way.

options.text: Mixing event handlers into HTML attributes makes the code harder to read and refactor
`onclick` attributes no longer work in modern browsers
`addEventListener` is faster because it runs on the server
`onclick` can only be used on `<a>` elements

questions.title: Fundamentals 2 – CSS
questions.explanation: Specificity from low to high: type → class → ID → inline style → `!important`. The ID selector wins.

options.text: Blue, because the type selector comes first
Green, because classes are meant for styling
Blue, green and red are mixed
Red, because the ID selector has the highest specificity here

questions.title: Fundamentals 2 – CSS
questions.explanation: When two rules have the same specificity, the one that comes last wins.

options.text: White, because the first rule wins
Neither, the conflict makes the browser ignore both rules
Grey, because with equal specificity the last rule wins
White, because `white` is a named colour and `grey` is not

questions.title: Fundamentals 2 – CSS
questions.text: What does the lesson say about using `!important`?
questions.explanation: `!important` overrides everything, but it is a sledgehammer. Find the conflicting rule in DevTools and fix it properly instead.

options.text: It is the recommended way to make sure a style is always applied
It is a bad smell: it usually means another rule is more specific than you realised
It only works on ID selectors
It makes the rule apply only on mobile devices

questions.title: Fundamentals 2 – CSS
questions.text: Where should almost all of the CSS of a real project live?
questions.explanation: Separate stylesheets keep structure and styling apart. `<style>` blocks are for small examples and prototypes, inline styles should be avoided.

options.text: In `style` attributes on each element
In a `<style>` block at the bottom of the `<body>`
In JavaScript, using `element.style`
In separate `.css` files, linked with a `<link>` tag

questions.title: Fundamentals 2 – CSS
questions.text:
Why should inline styles (`

`) be avoided?
questions.explanation: Changing a colour would mean editing every element by hand. Copy-pasting styles is where bugs and inconsistencies come from.

options.text: Browsers ignore inline styles when a stylesheet is present
Inline styles have the lowest specificity, so they never apply
There is no separation between structure and styling, and the same style has to be duplicated on every element
Inline styles only work in `<div>` elements

questions.title: Fundamentals 2 – CSS
questions.text: Which class name follows the naming advice from the lesson best?
questions.explanation: Name things by what they are, not how they look (`.warning` survives a redesign, `.red-text` does not). Use lowercase with dashes, and class names can't start with a number.

options.text: `.redText`
`.box2`
`.warning`
`.4-warning`

questions.title: Fundamentals 2 – CSS
questions.explanation: Custom properties always start with `--`, also when you read them with `var(--name)`.

options.text: CSS variables can't be used for backgrounds
Variables in `:root` are only available to the `<html>` element
The name inside `var()` must include the dashes: `var(--main-color)`
The variable must be declared inside the `button` rule

questions.title: Fundamentals 2 – CSS
questions.text: What is the main advantage of defining colours and spacing as CSS variables in `:root`?
questions.explanation: Variables are the basis of a design system: one source for colours, spacing and typography.

options.text: The page loads faster because variables are cached by the browser
Variables make CSS work in browsers without JavaScript
Variables give rules a higher specificity
You change a value in one place and everything that uses it updates, which keeps the design consistent

questions.title: Fundamentals 2 – CSS
questions.text:
```css
.tabledemo .tabledemo-cell { padding: 10px 16px; }
```
Which elements get the padding?
questions.explanation: A space between two selectors is a descendant combinator: the second element must sit inside the first.

options.text: Elements with class `tabledemo-cell` that are inside an element with class `tabledemo`
Every element that has both classes `tabledemo` and `tabledemo-cell`
Elements with class `tabledemo` and all elements with class `tabledemo-cell`
Only the first `tabledemo-cell` on the page

questions.title: Fundamentals 2 – CSS
questions.text: What does `padding: 16px 24px;` mean?
questions.explanation: Two values: top/bottom, then left/right. Four values go clockwise from the top.

options.text: 16px on the left and right, 24px on the top and bottom
16px on the top, 24px on the bottom
16px on the top and bottom, 24px on the left and right
16px of padding and 24px of margin

questions.title: Fundamentals 2 – CSS
questions.text: What is the difference between `padding` and `margin`?
questions.explanation: Padding is part of the box, margin is the space between boxes.

options.text: Padding is space inside the border (it gets the background colour), margin is space outside the border between elements
Padding is space outside the border, margin is space inside it
Padding is only for text, margin is only for images
There is no difference, they are aliases

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.text: What is the main difference between Flexbox and Grid?
questions.explanation: Flex arranges children in one direction; grid arranges them in rows and columns at the same time.

options.text: Flexbox handles vertical alignment exclusively, while Grid handles horizontal alignment exclusively.
Flexbox is used exclusively for legacy browsers, whereas Grid is exclusively supported on modern mobile devices.
Flexbox is designed for one-dimensional layouts (either a row or a column), whereas Grid is designed for two-dimensional layouts (rows and columns simultaneously).
Flexbox requires an external JavaScript library to calculate element sizes, whereas Grid is a native CSS specification.

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.text: You set `display: flex` on an element. Which elements are arranged by it?
questions.explanation: A layout mode is set on the parent and arranges its direct children. That is why your HTML structure decides which layouts are possible.

options.text: The element itself and all of its siblings
All descendants of the element, at every level
The direct children of the element
Only the first child of the element

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.text:
```css .highlight { width: 300px; height: 100px; background: navy; } ``` ```html

Some text here

``` The span stays as wide as its text. Why?
questions.explanation: Inline elements flow with the text. Use `display: inline-block` (or `block`) to make width and height apply.

options.text:
The `

` element overrides the width of all its children
`height` only works when `width` is given in percent
The background colour hides the extra width

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.text:
```css
.box { width: 300px; padding: 20px; border: 2px solid; }
```
Without any `box-sizing` rule, how wide is the box on screen?
questions.explanation: By default `width` is only the content: 300 + 2×20 padding + 2×2 border = 344px.

options.text: 300px
344px
322px
340px

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.text: What does `box-sizing: border-box` do?
questions.explanation: With `border-box`, `width: 300px` means the whole box is 300px; the content area shrinks to make room.

options.text: It adds a border to every element
It removes the margin from every element
It makes `width` include the padding and the border, so the whole box is exactly that width
It makes elements behave as block elements

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.text:
```css
nav { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; }
```
With the default `flex-direction: row`, what does `align-items: center` do?
questions.explanation: `justify-content` works on the main axis (horizontal in a row), `align-items` works on the cross axis (vertical in a row).

options.text: It centres the items vertically (on the cross axis)
It centres the items horizontally
It puts equal space between the items
It centres the text inside each item

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.text: Which CSS centres a child both horizontally and vertically inside its parent?
questions.explanation: With flexbox, `justify-content` centres on the main axis and `align-items` on the cross axis.

options.text: `.parent { text-align: center; vertical-align: middle; }`
`.child { margin: center; }`
`.parent { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; }`
`.parent { display: grid; grid-template-columns: center; }`

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.text:
```css
.layout { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr; }
```
What is the result?
questions.explanation: `1fr` means one fraction of the remaining space.

options.text: Two rows: one of 200px and one that fills the rest
Two columns of 200px each
Two columns: a fixed 200px column and a column that takes the remaining space
One column of 200px; `1fr` is ignored

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.explanation: The browser works out how many columns fit. It is responsive without a single media query.

options.text: It always creates exactly 4 columns of 250px
It creates one column of 250px and puts the rest of the cards in a second row
It only works when there is a media query for mobile
It creates as many columns as fit, each at least 250px wide and stretching to fill the row

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.text: A row of navigation links in a flex container overflows the screen on mobile. Which property lets the items continue on the next line?
questions.explanation: By default flex items stay on one line. `flex-wrap: wrap` allows them to wrap.

options.text: `flex-direction: row`
`align-items: stretch`
`justify-content: space-around`
`flex-wrap: wrap`

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.text: What does working **mobile-first** mean?
questions.explanation: Default = small viewport. Media queries add complexity as the screen gets bigger.

options.text: You write the default styles for small screens and add styles for larger screens in `min-width` media queries
You build a separate website for mobile devices
You write styles for desktop and hide elements on mobile with `display: none`
You only test on a phone and never on a desktop

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.explanation: `min-width: 768px` means: this CSS applies when the viewport is 768px or wider.

options.text: When the viewport is at most 768px wide
Only on devices with exactly 768px
Only when the page is printed
When the viewport is at least 768px wide

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.text: The root font size is 16px. How large is `1.5rem`?
questions.explanation: `rem` is relative to the root font size: 1.5 × 16 = 24px. (`em` is the one that depends on the current element.)

options.text: 1.5px
16px
Depends on the font size of the parent element
24px

questions.title: Fundamentals 3 – CSS layout
questions.text: What is the main difference between Bootstrap and Tailwind?
questions.explanation: Bootstrap = component library (`btn`, `card`). Tailwind = utility-first (`flex`, `pt-4`, `text-gray-700`).

options.text: Bootstrap gives pre-styled components and a grid, Tailwind gives small single-purpose utility classes that you combine in the HTML
Bootstrap is for CSS, Tailwind is for JavaScript
Bootstrap only works with Vue, Tailwind only works with React
There is no difference, Tailwind is the new name of Bootstrap

questions.title: Fundamentals 4 – JavaScript
questions.text: Which method would you use if you wanted to create a new array containing only the items that satisfy a specific condition?
questions.explanation: `filter` keeps the elements that pass a test and returns a new, possibly shorter array.

options.text: map()
forEach()
reduce()
filter()

questions.title: Fundamentals 4 – JavaScript
questions.text:
```js
const names = products.map(p => p.name);
```
What is `names`?
questions.explanation: `map` transforms every element and returns a new array of the same length. The original array is not changed.

options.text: The `products` array, with every product changed to its name
The name of the first product
`undefined`, because `map` does not return anything
A new array with the same length as `products`, containing the names

questions.title: Fundamentals 4 – JavaScript
questions.text:
```js
const total = products.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.price, 0);
```
What is the purpose of the `0`?
questions.explanation: `reduce` boils the array down to one value. The second argument is the starting value of the running total. Always provide it.

options.text: It is the index where reduce starts
It is the value returned when the array is empty and otherwise ignored
It limits the result to positive numbers
It is the starting value of the accumulator (`sum`)

questions.title: Fundamentals 4 – JavaScript
questions.text:
```js
const products = [
  { name: 'Laptop', price: 1200, inStock: true },
  { name: 'Phone', price: 800, inStock: false },
  { name: 'Tablet', price: 600, inStock: true },
];
const result = products
  .filter(p => p.inStock)
  .filter(p => p.price < 1000)
  .reduce((total, p) => total + p.price, 0);
```
What is `result`?
questions.explanation: In stock: Laptop and Tablet. Under 1000: Tablet. Sum of prices: 600.

questions.title: Fundamentals 4 – JavaScript
questions.text: What is a higher-order function?
questions.explanation: `map`, `filter` and `reduce` are higher-order functions: you pass them a function.

options.text: A function that is declared at the top of a file
A function that runs before all other functions
A function with more than three parameters
A function that takes another function as an argument (or returns one)

questions.title: Fundamentals 4 – JavaScript
questions.text: Which statement describes a **pure function**?
questions.explanation: No side effects (no global variables, no DOM changes) and the result depends only on the input.

options.text: A function that has no parameters
A function written with the arrow syntax
A function that only works on numbers
A function that always returns the same output for the same input and changes nothing outside itself

questions.title: Fundamentals 4 – JavaScript
questions.explanation: `map` does not mutate the original array (immutability). It returns a new array.

options.text: `undefined`

questions.title: Fundamentals 4 – JavaScript
questions.explanation: The braces are read as a function body, not as an object, and there is no `return`. To return an object literal, wrap it in parentheses: `(n) => ({ value: n })`.

options.text: `{ value: 5 }`
`undefined`
A syntax error

questions.title: Fundamentals 4 – JavaScript
questions.explanation: Every recursive function needs a base case, such as `if (n <= 0) return 1;`.

options.text: Functions are not allowed to call themselves
It has no stopping case, so it keeps calling itself until the program crashes
It should use `map` instead of `*`
Nothing, it correctly returns the factorial

questions.title: Fundamentals 4 – JavaScript
questions.text: What is logged by `console.log("5" + 3)`?
questions.explanation: With `+` and a string, JavaScript concatenates: `"53"`. This kind of weirdness is one reason the course uses TypeScript.

options.text: `NaN`
An error, because you can't add a string and a number

questions.title: Fundamentals 4 – JavaScript
questions.text: What is the difference between a multi-page application and a single-page application (SPA)?
questions.explanation: An SPA fetches only the data it needs and updates the page in place, while the URL and back button still work.

options.text: In an SPA the browser loads one HTML page and JavaScript updates the DOM on navigation; in a multi-page application the server sends a full new page on every click
An SPA has only one page of content; a multi-page application has several
A multi-page application needs a framework, an SPA does not
An SPA can't change the URL in the address bar

questions.title: Fundamentals 4 – JavaScript
questions.text: According to the lessons, what are the two things a frontend framework like Vue or React does for you?
questions.explanation: You declare what the screen should look like for the data; the framework does the DOM updates.

options.text: It writes your CSS and it hosts your website
It replaces HTML with JavaScript and it compiles your code to C#
It stores your data in a database and handles user logins
It lets you describe the UI as a function of state, and it updates the DOM efficiently when the state changes

questions.title: Fundamentals 4 – JavaScript
questions.text: Why does a modern frontend project need a build step (a tool like Vite)?
questions.explanation: The build tool follows the imports, converts TypeScript to JavaScript and produces a small set of optimised files.

options.text: Because browsers can only run one JavaScript file per page
Because HTML must be converted to JavaScript before a browser can show it
Because the build step uploads the code to the server
Because the browser doesn't understand TypeScript, and loading hundreds of separate files would be too slow
